slides.notes: Gr(2,3) is a two-dimensional manifold whose points are planes through the origin in three-dimensional Euclidean space. Finite colored patches are drawing windows onto infinite planes. The handbook uses the reverse notation Gr(n,k).

elements.html: A point can represent an entire plane.
Fix the dimension k. Let the subspace vary.

\[\mathrm{Gr}(k,n)=\{\mathcal S\subset\mathbb R^n:\dim\mathcal S=k\}\]A point is a linear subspace, not an individual vector in it.

All subspaces contain the origin.

Our notation: k first, ambient n second. We assume 0 < k < n.

elements.alt: Two bases of the same plane

slides.notes: Q is an n-by-k orthonormal representative. The equivalence includes the whole orthogonal group, including reflections: the Grassmannian here is unoriented. At 180 degrees in k=2, QO=-Q but the same plane is represented.

elements.html: Change the basis. Keep the point.
The coordinates inside a subspace are not part of its identity.

\[Q^\top Q=I_k,\qquad [Q]=\{QO:O\in O(k)\}\]Rotations, reflections, and column sign flips preserve the column space.

In the lab, rotate the arrows and watch the plane remain fixed.

Static example: a 90° basis rotation gives ‖Q − QO‖F = 2; the subspace distance is 0.

elements.alt: Two bases of the same plane

slides.notes: Stiefel dimension is nk-k(k+1)/2 for real matrices. O(k) has dimension k(k-1)/2; the quotient dimension is k(n-k). Reflections are discrete identifications and do not change this dimension count.

elements.html: Remove the degrees of freedom of the basis.
Stiefel keeps a frame. Grassmann keeps only its span.
\[nk-\frac{k(k+1)}2-\frac{k(k-1)}2\]Orthonormality removes k(k+1)/2 parameters; internal rotations remove k(k−1)/2.

Each orthonormal frame belongs to a whole family QO.

The quotient identifies that family with one subspace. Gr(2,3) has dimension 2.

slides.notes: The symmetric idempotent rank-k projectors are another representation of Gr(k,n). The trace equals rank because projector eigenvalues are zero or one. For a nonorthonormal full-rank B, use B(B^T B)^{-1}B^T instead of BB^T.

elements.html: The projector forgets the basis automatically.
Every k-dimensional subspace has exactly one orthogonal projector.
\[\widehat x=Px,\qquad x-Px\perp\operatorname{span}(Q)\]Px is the least-squares approximation of x within the subspace.

Q stores nk entries; P stores n² entries.

P is unique, but an orthonormal basis is usually cheaper computationally.

slides.notes: Real projective spaces parameterize one-dimensional linear subspaces. Gr(1,2) is topologically a circle after antipodal identification. Gr(1,3) is RP2 rather than S2. Orthogonal complementation identifies Gr(k,n) and Gr(n-k,n).

elements.html: A sphere picture needs an antipodal identification.

\[[u]=[-u],\qquad\|u\|=1\]Gr(1,2): unoriented lines in a plane.

Gr(1,3) ≅ ℝP²: sphere points u and −u represent the same line.

A plane through the origin is determined by its normal direction.

Normals n and −n describe the same plane.

Offset planes need affine geometry.

slides.notes: This example is exact for any real orthonormal Q. Orthogonal Procrustes can align representatives, but its distance convention still differs globally from the intrinsic geodesic distance.

elements.html: Matrix distance can report a change that never happened.
Two representatives may look far apart while the subspace is identical.
\[\|Q-(-Q)\|_F=2\sqrt{k}\]\[QQ^\top=(-Q)(-Q)^\top\]Basis distance is sensitive to signs and rotations.

\[d_g([Q],[-Q])=0\]Use principal angles or projector distances.

Never report raw basis error as subspace error without alignment.

slides.notes: Both bases are orthonormal. Singular values are nonnegative and sorted descending, so principal angles are sorted ascending. The first angle maximizes vector alignment; subsequent pairs add orthogonality constraints. In floating point clamp singular values to [0,1].

elements.html: The singular values of QᵀY remove both choices of basis.
\[Q^\top Y=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i)V^\top\]\[\theta_i=\arccos\sigma_i\]\[0\leq\theta_1\leq\cdots\leq\theta_k\leq\pi/2\]The corresponding principal vectors are columns of QU and YV.

elements.alt: Principal angles in two coordinate slices

slides.notes: dg is the canonical Grassmann geodesic distance. dp is the normalized projector Frobenius distance, sometimes called a chordal distance; EAS distinguishes projection and chordal conventions, so the formula is explicit. Equal k is assumed.

elements.html: Two useful distances. Two different geometries.
The normalization and angle units belong in the formula.
\[d_g=\sqrt{\sum_i\theta_i^2}\]\[d_p=\frac{\|QQ^\top-YY^\top\|_F}{\sqrt2}\]\[d_p=\sqrt{\sum_i\sin^2\theta_i}\]Angles in radians. For small angles, sin θ ≈ θ; globally these distances differ.

elements.alt: Principal angles in two coordinate slices

slides.notes: For alpha,beta in [0,pi/2], the two principal angles are alpha,beta sorted ascending. Orthogonality of the two coordinate slices provides an analytic validation case. Dimensions of the ambient space must be explicit in geometric illustrations.

elements.html: Two planes in ℝ³ must share a direction.
The experiment uses ℝ⁴ so that both principal angles can vary.
\[\dim(S\cap T)\geq\dim S+\dim T-3=1\]For two planes, θ₁ = 0; only θ₂ varies.

slides.notes: The horizontal tangent lift is n-by-k and has k(n-k) degrees of freedom. General Stiefel tangents satisfy Q^T Z+Z^T Q=0; Grassmann horizontal lifts satisfy the stronger Q^T Delta=0.

elements.html: A tangent points out of the current subspace.
Horizontal representatives remove motion that only changes the basis.

\[Q^\top\Delta=0\]\[\Pi_Q(Z)=(I-QQ^\top)Z\]Internal motion QΩ, with Ωᵀ = −Ω, changes the frame alone.

A horizontal Δ changes the Grassmannian point.

slides.notes: The compact formula with the identity correction handles rank-deficient tangents and n<2k. For horizontal Delta, Q^T U=0 for its nonzero singular directions. The horizontal metric is trace(Delta1^T Delta2); projector tangent metric has factor 1/2.

elements.html: Rotate the active directions with sines and cosines.
For a compact rank-r SVD Δ = UΣVᵀ, use the canonical metric.
\[Q(0)=Q,\quad\dot Q(0)=\Delta\]\[Q(t)^\top Q(t)=I_k\]Zero singular directions stay fixed.

The speed is ‖Δ‖F.

A sufficiently long geodesic is no longer a shortest path. Cut points matter when inverting the map.

slides.notes: For theta strictly below pi/2 the shortest subspace geodesic is unique. At pi/2, multiple shortest paths connect the endpoint lines; the demo chooses one. The vector sphere is a double cover of the real projective plane, not the manifold itself.

elements.html: Follow a geodesic between unoriented lines.
A great-circle arc is a representative path, with antipodal points identified.

\[q(t)=u\cos(t\theta)+w\sin(t\theta)\]\[w=\frac{v-u\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\]First choose the sign of v so uᵀv ≥ 0.

For 0 ≤ t ≤ 1: distance from the start = tθ.

At θ = 0, the path is constant.

slides.notes: The displayed log formula assumes equal dimensions and all principal angles strictly less than pi/2. The returned tangent exponential reaches the target subspace, not necessarily the exact input basis. See Handbook section 5 for cut locus and stable logarithm algorithms.

elements.html: The logarithm is local, not globally single-valued.
A principal angle of 90° marks the boundary of a unique shortest logarithm.
\[Z=(I-QQ^\top)Y(Q^\top Y)^{-1}\]\[Z=U\Sigma V^\top\]\[\operatorname{Log}_{[Q]}[Y]=U\arctan(\Sigma)V^\top\]This gives a horizontal tangent representative.

If a principal angle is π/2, QᵀY is singular.

There are multiple minimizing logarithms. Near the boundary, this inverse-based expression is numerically fragile.

Use robust algorithms from the handbook.

slides.notes: For a horizontal Delta, (Q+Delta)^T(Q+Delta)=I+Delta^T Delta is positive definite, so Q+Delta retains full column rank. The demo uses twice-reorthogonalized modified Gram-Schmidt on tiny matrices and Armijo backtracking.

elements.html: An orthonormalization can be a local step.
A retraction matches the exponential to first order; it is cheaper to compute.

QR returns an orthonormal frame.

Column sign conventions do not change the represented subspace.

A tangent is local. Use a line search or a trust region to control the optimization step.

QR retraction is generally not the exact exponential.

slides.notes: Assume real symmetric covariance C and centered samples. The Euclidean derivative is -2CQ, then horizontal projection gives the displayed canonical gradient. The eigenspace solution follows the Rayleigh-Ritz principle. Boundary ties create nonunique optimal subspaces.

elements.html: Learn the subspace that retains the most variance.
C is the covariance of centered data; the representation Q is orthonormal.

\[f(QO)=f(Q)\]Only the span matters.

Reconstruction loss = tr(C) − tr(QᵀCQ).

The span of the k leading eigenvectors.

The subspace is unique if λk > λk+1, even when eigenvalues inside it are repeated.

slides.notes: This is a deterministic centered synthetic cloud of 96 Fourier-generated samples, not a Gaussian dataset or benchmark. Its covariance eigenvalues are exactly the configured values in exact arithmetic. Optimization uses the actual sample covariance. A stationary start can fail to reach the best eigenspace in general; this demonstration uses a specified nonstationary initial basis.

slides.notes: These are use cases of a subspace representation, not claims that every model in the named fields is Grassmannian. Complex formulas require conjugate transpose and the appropriate real part of the Hermitian tangent inner product.

Subspace tracking: follow a changing signal subspace.

Reduced models: represent a low-dimensional trial space.

Recognition: compare learned feature subspaces.
\[Q^H Q=I,\quad [Q]=\{QU:U\in U(k)\}\]\[\dim_{\mathbb R}\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(k,n)=2k(n-k)\]Use conjugate transpose and unitary changes of basis. The labs here are real.

slides.notes: Lusk and How, Global Data Association for SLAM with 3D Grassmannian Manifold Objects, arXiv:2205.08556v1. This extension is essential: directions alone do not represent object offsets. Graff(k,n) is not Gr(k,n) times an unrestricted R^n translation.

elements.html: SLAM objects are often displaced lines and planes.
The supplied paper uses the affine Grassmannian.

\[\mathcal A=b+\operatorname{span}(A)\]\[b_\perp=(I-AA^\top)b\]Line: k = 1. Plane: k = 2.

Moving b along the object does not change the affine subspace.

\[\dim\operatorname{Graff}(k,n)=(k+1)(n-k)\]

elements.alt: A plane displaced from the origin

slides.notes: Equations (2)-(5). A has orthonormal columns, A^T b_perp=0, so the final homogeneous column is orthogonal to the others and normalized. The paper compares objects of unequal dimension using the smaller number of principal angles. Same-k metric claims should not be silently extended to their union.

elements.html: Embed an affine object in one extra dimension.
A 3-D line becomes a 2-D linear subspace in ℝ⁴; a plane becomes a 3-D one.

\[Y=\begin{bmatrix}A&b_\perp/\eta\\0&1/\eta\end{bmatrix}\]\[\eta=\sqrt{1+\|b_\perp\|^2}\]\[\operatorname{Graff}(k,3)\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Gr}(k+1,4)\]Divide positions by a length scale ρ before embedding.

Compute singular values of Y₁ᵀY₂ and take the norm of the principal angles.

For mixed dimensions, retain min(k₁+1,k₂+1) angles.

Across dimensions, containment can give zero: this is a dissimilarity, not a separating metric.

slides.notes: These distinctions prevent frequent visualization and implementation errors. For the association paper, also distinguish same-type candidate edges from mixed-type within-scan comparisons and a dissimilarity across dimensions from a metric on a single fixed-k Grassmannian.

elements.html: Five distinctions keep the geometry honest.
Every one is visible somewhere in the experiments.

Basis ≠ subspace. Use equivalence classes.

Sphere ≠ Grassmannian. Identify antipodes for real lines.

Linear ≠ affine. Offsets need additional coordinates.

Path length ≠ shortest distance after a cut point.

Count ≠ weighted density in the association objective.

Also state radians, projector normalization, and real versus complex conventions.

slides.notes: The gradient expression assumes a smooth right-orthogonally invariant objective and the canonical horizontal Frobenius metric. Units of angles in distance calculations are radians. For affine association, additionally shift corresponding anchors before homogeneous embedding and keep the scale fixed across scans.
